passages.title: Which cue goes with which consequence
paragraphs: Two events that occur together are not always learned about with equal ease. A laboratory tested whether the ease of an association depends on what kind of cue is paired with what kind of consequence. Ninety-six rats, matched for weight and water deprivation, were assigned at random to four groups of 24. In a single conditioning session every animal drank for ten minutes from a spout, and every animal then received one consequence. For Groups 1 and 2 the spout delivered water flavoured with a sweetener the animals had never tasted. For Groups 3 and 4 the spout delivered plain water, and each lick was accompanied by a click and a flash of light. Groups 1 and 3 then received an injection of an emetic agent that produces several hours of gastric malaise. Groups 2 and 4 received a brief shock to the floor of the cage.

Three days later each animal was returned to the apparatus for a ten-minute test with its own cue present and no consequence of any kind. An automated counter recorded licks, and the technician who weighed the animals and transcribed the counts did not know which group an animal belonged to. Licking during the minute before the test, with the spout dry, did not differ across groups. Table 1 gives the mean licks per minute during the conditioning session, the mean during the test, and the reduction from the session rate. A further 24 animals, run alongside the four groups, drank the flavoured water and received no consequence of any kind; they licked at 59 per minute at test.

Drinking fell by 80 percent where a flavour had been followed by malaise and by 75 percent where an audiovisual cue had been followed by shock. The two crossed pairings produced small reductions, although the cues were the same, the consequences were the same, and every animal had exactly one pairing of one cue with one consequence. The investigators argued that an association is not a blank slot waiting for whatever two events arrive together, and that a species arrives with a bias about which cues are worth treating as signals for which kinds of trouble.

passages.title: Span, similar sounds and a repeated syllable
paragraphs: How many items a person can hold for a few seconds depends on how the items are held. Forty-eight adult volunteers were tested on letter span. Lists of consonants were shown one at a time on a screen at one letter per second, and the volunteer wrote the list in order as soon as the last letter disappeared. Span was defined as the longest list length the volunteer reproduced in the correct order on at least two of three attempts. Two factors were varied within each volunteer. Lists were drawn either from a set of letters that rhyme, so that their names sound alike, or from a set whose names sound quite different. During half the blocks the volunteer said the syllable da aloud twice a second from the moment the first letter appeared until the last had gone, a task known as articulatory suppression; during the other half the volunteer was silent.

Every volunteer completed all four blocks, and the order of the four was assigned by a Latin square so that each block appeared equally often in each position across the sample. The letters were shown, not spoken, and no volunteer reported reading the lists aloud. Table 1 gives the mean span in each condition. The difference between the two list types, which is the cost of having to hold items that sound alike, was 1.6 items when the volunteers were silent and 0.2 items when they were suppressing articulation.

Suppression lowered span under both list types, but it did more than that: it removed almost all of the penalty for similar sounds. The investigators read this as evidence that a visually presented letter is ordinarily recoded into a sound-based form and kept there by silent rehearsal, which is why letters that sound alike interfere with one another. Occupying the mouth with an irrelevant syllable prevents that recoding, so the list is held in some other way, and the acoustic similarity of the letters stops mattering. They noted that span never fell below four items in any condition, so no floor on the measure can explain the result.

passages.title: How long an afterimage lasts
paragraphs: Stare at a saturated colour, look away at a blank grey card, and a coloured ghost appears on the card. Forty observers with normal colour vision were seated in a dim room and fixated a small cross at the centre of a coloured square that filled five degrees of the visual field. The square was either a saturated red or a saturated blue of matched luminance. Adaptation lasted 10, 20, 30 or 40 seconds, and the four durations and two colours were presented in a random order across trials, with two minutes of grey between trials. At the end of adaptation the square was replaced by a neutral grey field, and the observer held a key down for as long as any coloured ghost remained visible. Figure 1 gives the mean duration of the reported afterimage.

Observers were also asked to match the hue of the afterimage by turning a dial that moved a patch around a colour circle. After the red square, every observer set the dial in the blue-green region; after the blue square, every observer set it in the yellow region. A green square, used in a short additional block, produced settings in the red region. No observer reported an afterimage in the same hue as the square just viewed, and the match was made within two seconds of the square's disappearance in every case.

The duration of the afterimage grew with the length of adaptation, steeply between 10 and 30 seconds and then much less steeply. The investigators pointed out that neither the hue of the afterimage nor its growth with adaptation follows from the number of cone types alone: three cone classes can code a wavelength, but they do not by themselves predict that the ghost of a red field is blue-green. What does predict it is a stage that takes differences between cone signals, so that a cell excited by long wavelengths is inhibited by middle ones. Hold one side of such a pair at a steady level and its response declines; remove the stimulus and the pair settles back through the opposite sign.

passages.title: A pen, a cartoon and a rating
paragraphs: A cover story allows a facial posture to be imposed without naming what it is for. One hundred and fifty undergraduates were told that the study concerned how people manage a task with the hands occupied. Each was assigned at random to hold a pen between the teeth, which draws the corners of the mouth back and contracts the muscle that raises them in a smile; to hold it between pursed lips, which prevents that contraction; or to hold it in the non-dominant hand. While holding the pen the participant rated twelve single-panel cartoons for funniness on a scale from 1, not at all funny, to 9, extremely funny.

A second factor was crossed with the first. Half the participants in each pen position were given the coordination cover story and nothing else. The other half were told, before the cartoons appeared, that the study examined whether the position of the face changes how amusing something seems. Nothing else differed between these halves: the same cartoons were shown in the same order, and the pen was held in the same way for the same length of time. Table 1 gives the mean funniness rating in each of the six cells. The standard deviation of ratings, pooled across cells, was 2.0 scale points.

Where the purpose was not disclosed, the teeth group rated the cartoons 1.6 scale points funnier than the lips group, with the hand group between them. Where the purpose was disclosed, the three positions differed by at most 0.2 scale points. The investigators treated the first pattern as evidence that a bodily change contributes to the experience that is reported, and the second as evidence about how that contribution is used: a participant who has been told what the pen is for has an alternative source to which the feeling in the face can be assigned, and assigns it there rather than to the cartoon.

passages.title: Eight sessions for a fear of enclosed spaces
paragraphs: Ninety adults who met criteria for a specific phobia of enclosed spaces, all of whom reported avoiding lifts and small rooms for at least a year, were assigned at random in equal numbers to three arms. The first arm received eight weekly sessions of graded exposure: a hierarchy was built from the least to the most feared situation, and the patient remained in each situation, without distraction and without leaving, until the fear she reported had fallen by half. The second arm received eight weekly sessions of applied relaxation, in which breathing and muscle relaxation were taught and practised but no feared situation was entered. The third arm was placed on a waiting list and offered treatment after week eight.

Avoidance was scored on a 40-point inventory at entry and at week eight by an assessor who did not know the arm. A patient counted as a responder if her score fell by at least half. Every patient also completed an approach test at week eight, walking towards a windowless room while her heart rate was recorded; the peak rate reached is given in Table 1. Three patients withdrew, one from each arm, and were counted as non-responders in the arm to which they had been assigned.

Twenty-one of the thirty patients offered exposure responded, against twelve of thirty offered relaxation and six of thirty on the waiting list. The investigators noted that the relaxation arm improved on the waiting list, and suggested that what exposure adds is not the reduction of arousal but the disconfirmation of an expectation: the patient discovers that the enclosed room does not produce the catastrophe she predicted, and the avoidance that has prevented that discovery is no longer performed. They added that relaxation can itself become something the patient believes she must do before entering a lift.

passages.title: How far away the instruction comes from
paragraphs: One hundred and twenty adults answered an advertisement for a study of how distraction affects learning. Each was told that the person in the next room, in fact a member of staff following a script, would attempt a word task, and that the participant was to deliver a burst of unpleasant noise through headphones after every error, moving up one level on a twenty-level dial each time. The levels were labelled from faint to very severe. No noise in fact reached the member of staff, whose protests were recorded in advance and played at fixed levels; participants were told so at a full debriefing, and nobody declined to have their data used.

Participants were assigned at random, thirty to each of four conditions, which differed only in where the instruction to continue came from. In the first the experimenter sat beside the participant. In the second the experimenter sat at the far end of the same room and could not see the dial. In the third the experimenter gave the instruction by telephone from another building. In the fourth no experimenter was present at any point: the instruction to continue was played from a recording made by the same experimenter. The outcome was the proportion who reached level twenty, shown in Figure 1; the mean highest level reached was 18.4, 16.9, 13.2 and 11.6 in the four conditions in that order.

Twenty-four of the thirty participants seated beside the experimenter reached level twenty, as did eighteen of those with the experimenter across the room, nine of those instructed by telephone and six of those instructed by a recording. The scripted protests, the dial, the headphones and the word task were identical throughout, so the only thing that varied was the instructing person's presence. The investigators argued that what carries an instruction of this kind is not its content but the standing of whoever gives it, and that standing is something that decays with distance.

passages.title: Reading the case for a new fee
paragraphs: One hundred and sixty students read a one-page message arguing that their university should introduce a transport fee that would fund a bus service. Two features of the situation were crossed. The quality of the argument was either strong, in which case the message gave costed figures for the service, the fare saving per student and the results of a trial elsewhere, or weak, in which case it asserted that the fee was modern, that other places were doing something similar and that opponents had not thought it through. Personal relevance was manipulated by the date the fee was said to begin: either at the start of the next term, which would affect every reader, or in ten years, by which time no reader would still be enrolled.

Students were assigned at random to the four combinations, forty to each. After reading, each rated agreement with the proposal on a scale from 1 to 9 and then listed every thought that had occurred while reading, which two coders, blind to condition, sorted into thoughts about the content of the argument and thoughts about anything else. Table 1 gives the mean agreement rating and the mean number of content-related thoughts in each cell. No student was told anything about the source of the message, and no photograph or name accompanied it.

The quality of the argument made a difference of 3.2 scale points where the fee was to begin next term and a difference of 0.4 scale points where it was to begin in ten years. The count of content-related thoughts followed relevance rather than quality: students for whom the fee was imminent listed about three times as many such thoughts as students for whom it was distant. The investigators concluded that a message is not processed in one fixed way, and that whether its content governs the attitude it produces depends on whether the reader has a reason to work through it.

passages.title: A label on the same account
paragraphs: Six hundred adults recruited from a national online panel each read one vignette describing a man of 28 who had withdrawn from his friends, slept badly for months and sometimes heard a voice that others could not hear. The three versions of the vignette were identical in every sentence describing what the man did and felt. They differed only in the final line, which stated either that he had been given a diagnosis of schizophrenia, or that he had been told he had a mental illness, or that he was going through a stressful period in his life. Two hundred respondents, assigned at random, read each version.

Each respondent then completed a social distance scale of eight items, scored from 0 to 24, on which a higher score means a greater wish to keep the man at a distance; stated whether she would recommend that he see a mental health professional; stated whether she would be unwilling to have him as a next-door neighbour; and stated whether she thought his difficulties were caused by a disease of the brain. Table 1 gives the results. Respondents were not told that other versions existed, and the panel is not a probability sample of the adult population.

The diagnostic label raised both the proportion recommending professional help and the proportion unwilling to live next door. It also raised the proportion attributing the difficulties to a disease of the brain from 22 percent to 68 percent. The investigators observed that an account of symptoms acquires something when a name is attached to it that it did not carry before, and that the something is not simply a judgement of severity, since the described conduct was held constant. They also observed that what a respondent says she would do with a neighbour is not what she does, and that a man deciding whether to consult anyone must weigh the same reactions the study measured.

passages.title: Three levels of schooling across two generations
paragraphs: A national survey interviewed 4,000 adults aged between 40 and 49, an age by which education is almost always complete. Each respondent reported her own highest qualification and the highest qualification held by either parent, coded into three levels: no formal qualification, a school certificate, and a degree. Interviewers were trained to probe for the parent's qualification rather than accept a first answer, and the sample was weighted to the age distribution of the population. Of the respondents, 34 percent came from a household in which neither parent held a qualification, 41 percent from a household whose highest qualification was a school certificate, and 25 percent from a household in which a parent held a degree.

Table 1 reports, for each level of parental qualification, the percentage of respondents at each level of their own. Each row is a percentage of the respondents from that origin, so each row sums to 100. Sixty percent of respondents whose parent held a degree held a degree themselves, four times the 15 percent found among respondents whose parents held no qualification. Across the whole cohort 33 percent held a degree, against the 25 percent of parental households in which someone did.

The survey is cross-sectional: every respondent was interviewed once, and the parental figure is a report by the respondent rather than a record. The investigators were careful about what such a table can and cannot show. It records where people from each origin ended up, which is a description of destinations rather than a mechanism; nothing in it distinguishes an advantage carried in the home from an advantage conferred by the schools that children of educated parents attend. They noted that the share holding degrees rose between the generations, so that some of the upward movement reflects a change in the number of places available rather than an exchange of positions between families.

Two further facts about the cohort were recorded. Each respondent gave her place of birth: 18 percent of the 4,000, or 720 respondents, had migrated to the country after the age of sixteen, and for those respondents the parental qualification is one held in another country's system. The register from which the sample was drawn also gives the size of each ten-year birth cohort. The respondents' cohort, those born across the decade the survey covers, numbers 520,000 people, a fifth smaller than the 650,000 in the cohort born ten years earlier; the statistical office attributes that difference to the fall in the birth rate across the intervening decade and not to emigration, which was slight in both cohorts. The investigators observed that a cohort interviewed once in middle age is not the cohort that was born: deaths have removed some of its members and arrivals from abroad have added others, so its composition at interview is the product of births, deaths and migration together.

passages.title: Rating ninety occupations
paragraphs: Standing at work is measured, when it is measured at all, by asking people. A survey gave each of 1,200 respondents a list of 30 occupations drawn from a pool of 90 and asked them to place each one on a ladder from 0, the lowest standing in the community, to 100, the highest. Every occupation was rated by about 400 respondents, and the mean rating became that occupation's prestige score. The 90 occupations were then matched to administrative data giving the mean years of schooling of people working in them and their median annual earnings. Two further variables were recorded for each occupation: the percentage of its workers who belonged to a union, and the percentage of respondents who described the occupation as middle class.

The unit of analysis in Table 1 is the occupation, not the person, so each correlation is computed across 90 occupations. The prestige scores were also split: the ratings from odd-numbered respondents were correlated with those from even-numbered respondents, which gave a coefficient of 0.92. The investigators used that figure to argue that the ladder is answered consistently, and were explicit that consistency of this kind speaks to whether a measure repeats itself and not to whether it captures standing in the community.

Prestige tracked schooling more closely than it tracked pay. Several occupations sat well away from the line relating the two: some requiring long training were rated high and paid in the bottom quarter of the 90, and a few requiring little schooling were paid in the top quarter and rated below the middle. The investigators took this as a reason to keep the dimensions of standing apart when social class is measured, rather than collapsing schooling, earnings and prestige into a single index and assuming that an occupation sits at the same height on all three.
