questions.stem: In Group 1, which pairing of terms correctly identifies elements of the procedure?

choices.A: The flavour is the unconditioned stimulus and the malaise is the conditioned response.
choices.B: The injection is the conditioned stimulus and the reduced drinking is the unconditioned response.
choices.C: The flavour is the conditioned stimulus and the malaise after the injection is the conditioned response.
choices.D: The flavour is the conditioned stimulus and the reduced drinking at test is the conditioned response.

questions.explanation: The flavour began as a neutral stimulus and acquired its power only by being paired with the injection, so it is the conditioned stimulus; the emetic agent is the unconditioned stimulus, and the malaise it produces is the unconditioned response. What the flavour alone comes to produce, the fall in drinking from 60 to 12 licks per minute, is the conditioned response.

wrong.A: This reverses the two stimuli. The flavour had never been paired with anything before the session, so it cannot be the stimulus that produces malaise without learning.
wrong.B: The injection produces malaise without any training, which makes it the unconditioned stimulus, and the fall in drinking is what had to be learned rather than a reflex.
wrong.C: The malaise is produced directly by the emetic agent, so it is the unconditioned response; the animals were never made ill by the flavour alone.

questions.stem: The investigators argue that a species arrives with a bias about which cues signal which consequences. Which term names that claim?

choices.A: stimulus generalisation, the spread of a response to cues resembling the trained one
choices.B: higher-order conditioning, the use of a trained cue to train a second one
choices.C: latent inhibition, the slower conditioning of a cue already made familiar
choices.D: biological preparedness, an inherited readiness to associate particular cues with particular outcomes

questions.explanation: Preparedness is the claim that associability is not uniform: a species inherits a readiness to treat certain cues as signals for certain consequences. A flavour paired with malaise and an audiovisual cue paired with pain are the prepared pairings here, which is why the crossed cells learned so little from the same number of trials.

wrong.A: Generalisation concerns responding to a cue similar to the trained one; every animal was tested with its own cue, so no spread to a new cue is at issue.
wrong.B: Higher-order conditioning requires an already conditioned stimulus to serve as the consequence, and here every consequence was an injection or a shock.
wrong.C: Latent inhibition describes slow learning about a familiar cue, but the flavour was new to every animal and the click and light were equally new.

questions.stem: Group 1 animals are given ten further sessions with the flavoured water and no injection, after which their drinking has returned to 60 licks per minute. They are then left in their home cages for two weeks and offered the flavoured water again. Drinking will most likely:

choices.A: stay at 60 licks per minute, because the ten unreinforced sessions have erased the association
choices.B: fall to about 12 licks per minute, because the original learning is unaffected by what followed it
choices.C: fall somewhat below 60 licks per minute, because an extinguished response recovers after a rest interval
choices.D: rise above 60 licks per minute, because the flavour now signals that no injection is coming

questions.explanation: Extinction suppresses a conditioned response without destroying what was learned, and after an interval with no exposure the response returns in weaker form, which is spontaneous recovery. Drinking should therefore fall below the 60 licks per minute reached at the end of extinction, but not back to the 12 seen at the first test.

wrong.A: This treats extinction as erasure. If the association were destroyed, the response could not reappear after a rest, which is exactly what spontaneous recovery shows it does.
wrong.B: A return to the original level would mean the ten unreinforced sessions had no effect at all, whereas recovery after extinction is reliably partial.
wrong.D: Drinking above the group's own session rate would require the flavour to have become an appetitive signal, and nothing in the procedure pairs it with anything good.

questions.stem: What does the group that drank the flavoured water and received no consequence establish?

choices.A: that the emetic agent suppresses drinking whether or not a cue precedes it
choices.B: that the suppression in Group 1 cannot be attributed to the shock
choices.C: that the suppression in Group 1 is not simply wariness of an unfamiliar taste
choices.D: that the flavour and the audiovisual cue were equally detectable before conditioning

questions.explanation: A new flavour can depress drinking on its own, so without this group a fall in Group 1 could be put down to the novelty of the sweetener rather than to its pairing with malaise. The group drank at 59 licks per minute, near the 60 of the conditioning session, which leaves the pairing as the explanation for Group 1's fall to 12.

wrong.A: That would require a group given the injection with no cue at all; this group received no injection, so it says nothing about the agent's direct effect.
wrong.B: Group 1 never received a shock, so a shock was never a candidate explanation for its behaviour and needs no control group.
wrong.D: Matching the detectability of two cues would require measuring responses to each cue before any pairing, which no group in the study provides.

questions.stem: Using the test rates in Table 1, how large is the interaction between cue and consequence, taken as the difference between the two differences in test licks per minute?

choices.A: 0 licks per minute
choices.B: 36 licks per minute
choices.C: 39 licks per minute
choices.D: 72 licks per minute

questions.explanation: Within the flavour cue, shock minus emetic is 48 minus 12, or 36 licks per minute. Within the audiovisual cue it is 15 minus 51, or minus 36. Subtracting the second difference from the first, 36 less negative 36, gives an interaction of 72 licks per minute. An interaction this large with no main effect of either factor is what a crossed pattern looks like.

wrong.A: This adds the two signed differences instead of subtracting one from the other, so the two halves of the crossover cancel and a large interaction is reported as none.
wrong.B: This is one simple effect on its own, the 36 licks per minute separating the two flavour groups, and an interaction needs both simple effects compared.
wrong.C: This is 51 minus 12, the gap between the two groups given the emetic agent, which compares cues at one level of consequence rather than comparing differences.

questions.stem: Saying the syllable da twice a second while the letters are shown is thought to occupy which part of the memory system?

choices.A: the visuospatial sketchpad, which holds the shapes and positions of the letters
choices.B: the articulatory rehearsal process that refreshes the phonological store
choices.C: the central executive, which divides attention between two tasks at once
choices.D: the long-term store, from which the names of the letters must be retrieved

questions.explanation: Repeating an irrelevant syllable aloud ties up the articulatory process that would otherwise rehearse the list silently and keep the phonological store refreshed. That is why suppression lowers span under both list types and, more tellingly, removes the penalty for letters that sound alike.

wrong.A: The sketchpad holds visual and spatial material; occupying it would not explain why an effect that depends on how the letters sound disappears.
wrong.C: A general demand on attention would lower both spans without touching the similarity effect, which fell from 1.6 items to 0.2 items.
wrong.D: Retrieving letter names from long-term knowledge is required in every condition, including the silent ones, so it cannot be what suppression interferes with.

questions.stem: By how many items does articulatory suppression reduce the cost of holding letters that sound alike?

choices.A: 1.8 items
choices.B: 1.6 items
choices.C: 1.4 items
choices.D: 0.2 items

questions.explanation: The cost of similar-sounding letters is 6.4 minus 4.8, or 1.6 items, when the volunteers are silent, and 4.6 minus 4.4, or 0.2 items, when they are suppressing articulation. The reduction in that cost is 1.6 minus 0.2, which is 1.4 items.

wrong.A: This adds the two similarity effects, 1.6 and 0.2, instead of subtracting the smaller from the larger, and so reports more reduction than the whole effect ever was.
wrong.B: This is the similarity effect in the silent condition read as though suppression had abolished it entirely, but 0.2 items of it remain.
wrong.D: This is the similarity effect that survives under suppression, which is what is left rather than what was removed.

questions.stem: Which account best explains why suppression removes almost all of the penalty for letters that sound alike?

choices.A: Suppression lowers span to the floor of the measure, leaving no room for a further penalty to show itself.
choices.B: Letters that sound alike are harder to see on a screen, and suppression gives the eyes more time to inspect them.
choices.C: Suppression prevents the visually presented letters from being recoded into a sound-based form, so their sounds can no longer interfere.
choices.D: Suppression transfers the list to long-term memory, where items are stored by meaning and sound plays no part.

questions.explanation: The penalty exists because letters seen on a screen are ordinarily turned into a sound-based code and rehearsed there, and codes that sound alike blur together. Blocking articulation prevents the recoding, so the list is held in some other form and the acoustic similarity of the names stops mattering.

wrong.A: A floor effect is ruled out in the passage: span stayed above four items in every condition, so there was room for a penalty to appear.
wrong.B: The two sets of letters were equally legible, and suppression does not change the one-letter-per-second rate at which they were shown.
wrong.D: A list recalled seconds after presentation does not need to be transferred to long-term storage, and meaning-based storage would not be disrupted by saying a syllable aloud.

questions.stem: Why were the four blocks assigned to positions by a Latin square?

choices.A: Practice and fatigue across the session would otherwise be confounded with condition.
choices.B: It equates the two sets of letters for how often they occur in written English.
choices.C: It keeps each volunteer from working out what the study is about.
choices.D: It makes the four means independent, which the statistical test requires.

questions.explanation: Every volunteer completed all four blocks, so whichever condition came first would benefit least from practice and whichever came last would suffer most from fatigue. Rotating the four conditions through the four positions equally often across the sample spreads those order effects evenly instead of letting them accumulate in one condition.

wrong.B: Letter frequency is a property of the two stimulus sets and is unaffected by the order in which blocks are run; it would have to be controlled when the sets were built.
wrong.C: Order rotation does nothing to hide the manipulation, and volunteers who say a syllable aloud in half the blocks can hardly miss that something is being varied.
wrong.D: Four measurements from the same person are not independent whatever their order, which is why a within-subject analysis is used instead.

questions.stem: According to Figure 1, the afterimage of the red square after 30 seconds of adaptation lasted how many times as long as the afterimage of the red square after 10 seconds?

choices.A: 2.6 times
choices.B: 2.0 times
choices.C: 1.2 times
choices.D: 0.5 times

questions.explanation: The solid line reads 7.2 seconds at 30 seconds of adaptation and 3.6 seconds at 10 seconds. The ratio is 7.2 divided by 3.6, which is 2.0, so doubling occurs between 10 and 30 seconds of adaptation and almost nothing is added between 30 and 40.

wrong.A: This divides the red value at 30 seconds by the blue value at 10 seconds, 7.2 by 2.8, which mixes the two curves rather than comparing two adaptation times on one.
wrong.C: This divides the red value at 30 seconds by the blue value at the same time, 7.2 by 6.1, which compares the two squares instead of two adaptation times.
wrong.D: This divides the shorter duration by the longer, which gives the ratio the other way round and describes 10 seconds as a fraction of 30.

questions.stem: Which mechanism best explains why the red square produced an afterimage that observers matched in the blue-green region?

choices.A: A channel that is excited by long wavelengths and inhibited by middle ones adapts while red is viewed and responds in the opposite direction when red is removed.
choices.B: Grey light stimulates all three cone classes equally, so the class with the longest wavelength peak dominates the response to the grey field.
choices.C: The cones sensitive to long wavelengths are bleached, leaving the rods, which signal blue-green at the light levels used.
choices.D: The signal from the retina is inverted in the lateral geniculate nucleus whenever the eyes move to a new fixation point.

questions.explanation: Opponent coding takes differences between cone signals, so one cell carries red against green and another blue against yellow. Steady red viewing drives the red-green channel in one direction and its response declines; when the square goes, the channel settles back through the opposite sign, which is seen as blue-green.

wrong.B: Equal stimulation of the three cone classes is what makes a field look grey, and nothing about it would favour the long-wavelength class or produce a coloured ghost.
wrong.C: Rods do not carry hue information at all, and the room was dim but not dark enough to remove cone function; the observers matched hues reliably throughout.
wrong.D: Observers held fixation on a central cross, and an inversion tied to eye movements would not explain why the ghost's hue is the complement of the square's.

questions.stem: Which description of colour coding is consistent with both the hue matches and what is known of the visual system?

choices.A: Opponent coding occurs at the cones and trichromatic coding at the ganglion cells.
choices.B: Opponent coding occurs at every stage, and no trichromatic stage is involved.
choices.C: Trichromatic coding occurs in the cortex, the retina signalling only brightness.
choices.D: Trichromatic coding occurs at three cone classes, with opponent coding at stages after them.

questions.explanation: The two accounts describe different stages rather than competing for one. Three cone classes with overlapping sensitivities code wavelength at the receptors, and cells after the receptors take differences between those signals, which is what makes complementary afterimages and the absence of a reddish green possible.

wrong.A: This puts the two stages the wrong way round: the three classes of cone are the receptors, and the difference-taking cells lie after them.
wrong.B: Without three classes of receptor with different spectral sensitivities there would be nothing from which differences could be taken.
wrong.C: A retina that signalled brightness alone could not support the hue matches observers made, which were made within two seconds of the square's disappearance.

questions.stem: Which change to the procedure would be expected to have the LEAST effect on the measured duration of the afterimage?

choices.A: halving the luminance of the coloured square
choices.B: asking observers to press a key once the ghost has gone rather than hold one down while it lasts
choices.C: letting observers move their eyes freely over the square during adaptation
choices.D: shortening adaptation from 30 seconds to 10 seconds

questions.explanation: The duration depends on how strongly and how locally the opponent channels have been driven. How the observer signals the end of the ghost is a matter of the response, not of adaptation, so either way of marking that moment leaves the measured duration essentially unchanged.

wrong.A: Luminance determines how hard the channels are driven, and a dimmer square produces a weaker and shorter-lived afterimage.
wrong.C: Free eye movements spread the adapting light across different retinal regions, so no region is strongly adapted and the ghost is faint and brief.
wrong.D: Figure 1 shows duration falling from 7.2 seconds to 3.6 seconds for the red square across exactly this change, the largest effect in the study.

questions.stem: The pattern in the undisclosed cells is most often cited in support of which account of emotion?

choices.A: the Cannon-Bard account, in which the bodily response and the feeling arise at once and independently
choices.B: the Yerkes-Dodson relation, in which performance is best at a moderate level of arousal
choices.C: the Schachter-Singer account, in which arousal is interpreted by reference to the situation
choices.D: the James-Lange account, in which the bodily change contributes to the feeling that is reported

questions.explanation: A posture imposed before any cartoon appeared changed how funny the cartoons were rated, so a peripheral bodily change fed into the reported experience rather than merely following it. That direction of travel, from the body to the feeling, is what the James-Lange account claims.

wrong.A: If the bodily change and the feeling were independent, imposing the facial posture could not have moved the ratings by 1.6 scale points.
wrong.B: The Yerkes-Dodson relation concerns how arousal affects performance on a task, and no performance measure was taken here.
wrong.C: A two-factor account needs arousal that the participant then labels from the situation, but the manipulation was a muscle posture and the situation was held constant across pen positions.

questions.stem: Using Table 1 and the pooled standard deviation, what is the standardised difference between the teeth and lips groups in the undisclosed condition?
questions.explanation: A standardised difference divides the difference between two means by the pooled standard deviation. Here that is 6.2 minus 4.6, or 1.6 scale points, divided by 2.0 scale points, which gives 0.80.

wrong.A: This divides the difference of 1.6 by the teeth group's mean of 6.2 rather than by the standard deviation, which yields a proportion of a mean and not a standardised effect.
wrong.B: This uses the teeth group against the hand group, a difference of 0.8 scale points, rather than the comparison the question specifies.
wrong.D: This multiplies the difference by the standard deviation instead of dividing by it, which makes the effect larger as the spread of the ratings grows.

questions.stem: Which account best explains why the three pen positions produced almost identical ratings when the purpose had been disclosed?

choices.A: The disclosed groups were asked to contract different muscles, so the posture manipulation did not take effect in them.
choices.B: Participants who know what the pen is for attribute the feeling in the face to the pen and discount it when judging the cartoon.
choices.C: Being told the hypothesis adds to the demands of the task, which lowers every rating by the same amount.
choices.D: Disclosure makes the cartoons seem funnier, which pushes all three groups up against the top of the nine-point scale.

questions.explanation: The bodily change is still there, but it is no longer taken as information about the cartoon: a participant who has been told the study is about facial posture has an alternative source to which the feeling can be assigned. Discounting of this kind leaves the three positions within 0.2 scale points of one another.

wrong.A: The passage states that the pen was held in the same way for the same length of time in both halves, so the posture itself did not differ.
wrong.C: An equal fall in every rating would leave the differences between pen positions intact, and it is those differences that disappeared.
wrong.D: The disclosed means sit between 5.3 and 5.5 on a nine-point scale, which is nowhere near a ceiling, and the teeth group's rating fell rather than rose.

questions.stem: A participant in the hand condition says afterwards that her heart was racing as she read the cartoons, and that she took the racing as a sign of how amusing they were. Her report best illustrates which account of emotion?

choices.A: a James-Lange account, in which each emotion follows from its own distinct bodily pattern
choices.B: a Cannon-Bard account, in which bodily changes make no contribution to what is felt
choices.C: a two-factor account, in which an unspecific bodily state is labelled from the situation the person is in
choices.D: a facial feedback account, in which the muscles of the face settle which emotion is experienced

questions.explanation: A racing heart is compatible with amusement, nervousness and several other states, so what decides the label is the situation to which the participant assigns it. That is the two-factor claim: arousal supplies the intensity and the appraisal of the setting supplies the name.

wrong.A: A James-Lange account requires a bodily pattern specific to the emotion, whereas a racing heart is exactly the unspecific state that could have been read several ways.
wrong.B: On this account the participant's arousal would be irrelevant to her judgement, yet she reports using it as evidence about the cartoons.
wrong.D: The participant held the pen in her hand, so no facial posture was imposed on her, and the report concerns her heart rather than her face.

questions.stem: A participant in the undisclosed teeth condition shows a strong contraction of the muscle that raises the corners of the mouth and still reports no amusement at all. Which conclusion does this best support?

choices.A: Peripheral feedback modulates an emotional experience rather than generating one by itself.
choices.B: Emotional experience is a purely cognitive appraisal to which the body contributes nothing.
choices.C: The muscles of the face are the sole determinant of what a person feels and reports.
choices.D: Feedback from the face requires an intact amygdala, which this participant presumably lacks.

questions.explanation: One participant whose face is in the right posture and who reports nothing shows that the posture is not sufficient on its own, while the group difference of 1.6 scale points shows it is not irrelevant either. Feedback shifts an experience that other things also determine.

wrong.B: A body that contributed nothing could not have moved the group means at all, and the teeth and lips groups differed by 1.6 scale points.
wrong.C: This is the claim the single participant contradicts, since her facial muscles were contracting while she reported no amusement.
wrong.D: Nothing in the study measures any brain structure, and a report of no amusement in one participant gives no grounds for inferring damage anywhere.

questions.stem: At week eight a patient from the exposure arm says that she can now stay in a small room until her fear subsides, whatever she feels on entering it. Which construct does that statement describe?

choices.A: self-esteem, the overall value a person places on herself as she measures herself against others
choices.B: an external locus of control, the sense that what happens to her is settled by forces outside her
choices.C: a self-schema for illness, the organised body of belief through which a person reads herself as a patient
choices.D: self-efficacy, her judgement that she can carry out the actions a particular situation demands of her

questions.explanation: Self-efficacy is a judgement about a specific capability: whether this person can do this thing in this situation. The statement is exactly that, and it is what graded exposure is meant to produce, since remaining in each situation until fear has fallen by half gives the patient evidence about what she can do. It is distinct both from the value she places on herself in general and from where she locates the causes of what happens to her.

wrong.A: Self-esteem is a global evaluation of one's own worth, and the patient is reporting what she can do in one kind of situation rather than what she takes herself to be worth.
wrong.B: An external locus of control is better illustrated by the relaxation arm, where the patient credits the ritual rather than herself for the absence of the catastrophe she predicted.
wrong.C: A self-schema organises beliefs about the kind of person one is, whereas the statement concerns one action in one place rather than a standing description of herself.

questions.stem: The investigators suggest that relaxation can become something the patient believes she must do before entering a lift. Why would that limit the benefit of the relaxation arm?

choices.A: It works as a safety behaviour, so the patient attributes the absence of catastrophe to the relaxation rather than to the lift.
choices.B: It lowers physiological arousal, and a fear response cannot be extinguished unless arousal remains high throughout.
choices.C: It acts as negative punishment of avoidance, which weakens the response the treatment is trying to strengthen.
choices.D: It was delivered without a blind assessor, so the arm's response rate is inflated relative to exposure.

questions.explanation: A safety behaviour supplies an alternative explanation for the good outcome, so the patient's prediction about the enclosed space is never actually tested. The belief that the lift would be dangerous without the ritual survives the experience intact, which is why the arm improved on the waiting list without matching exposure.

wrong.B: Extinction depends on meeting the feared situation without the expected harm, not on maintaining high arousal; the exposure arm ended with the lowest peak heart rate at 92 beats per minute.
wrong.C: Negative punishment means removing something valued, and a relaxation ritual that makes entry possible is not the removal of anything.
wrong.D: The passage states that the assessor did not know the arm, and in any case an inflated rate would not explain why relaxation did worse than exposure.

questions.stem: A woman screened for the trial reports that for six months she has had sudden surges of intense fear, lasting minutes, in many settings including her own home, each with palpitations and a conviction that she is about to die, and that she now worries about when the next surge will come. Which description fits her report best?

choices.A: a specific phobia, because her fear is severe enough to interfere with her daily life
choices.B: generalised anxiety disorder, because she worries about her condition much of the time
choices.C: a stress reaction, because the surges are brief and resolve without treatment
choices.D: panic disorder, because unexpected attacks recur in several settings and she now fears the attacks themselves

questions.explanation: Her fear is not cued by one object or situation; the attacks arrive unexpectedly across settings, including at home, and the apprehension that has developed is about further attacks. Recurrent unexpected attacks together with persistent concern about them is the pattern that distinguishes panic disorder, and it is not what the trial was recruiting.

wrong.A: A specific phobia requires fear cued by a particular object or situation, and severity alone does not make a fear specific.
wrong.B: The worry here is about the attacks rather than spread across many areas of life, which is what distinguishes generalised anxiety from panic.
wrong.C: Attacks recurring across six months with developing apprehension about them are not a transient reaction, whatever the duration of each episode.

questions.stem: How many patients must be offered exposure rather than placed on the waiting list for one additional responder at week eight?

choices.A: 1.4 patients
choices.B: 2.0 patients
choices.C: 3.3 patients
choices.D: 5.0 patients

questions.explanation: The number needed to treat is the reciprocal of the difference between the two response rates. Exposure responded at 70% and the waiting list at 20%, a difference of 50 percentage points, and the reciprocal of 0.50 is 2.0 patients.

wrong.A: This is the reciprocal of the exposure arm's own response rate, 1 divided by 0.70, which counts responders who would have responded on the waiting list as well.
wrong.C: This is the reciprocal of the 30 percentage point gap between exposure and relaxation, which answers a different comparison from the one asked.
wrong.D: This is the reciprocal of the waiting list's response rate, 1 divided by 0.20, which uses the comparison arm alone and ignores the treatment.

questions.stem: A participant seated beside the experimenter later said that he had kept going because the experimenter, not he, was running the study. Which process does his account describe?

choices.A: an agentic state, in which a person sees himself as carrying out another's intention rather than his own
choices.B: informational social influence, in which a person treats others as a source of evidence about reality
choices.C: deindividuation, in which a person loses the sense of being identifiable within a group
choices.D: internalisation, in which a person comes to hold the instructed view as his own conviction

questions.explanation: The shift of responsibility for the outcome onto the instructing person is what the agentic state names: the participant continues to act but no longer regards the act as his. The passage's own account, that what carries the instruction is the standing of whoever gives it, depends on there being someone to hand responsibility to.

wrong.B: Informational influence operates when a person is uncertain about the facts and copies others to get them right, and nothing here was uncertain about the noise levels.
wrong.C: Deindividuation requires a group within which the person is anonymous, and each participant was tested alone with at most one other person present.
wrong.D: Internalisation means the person adopts the view as his own, whereas this participant distances himself from what he did.

questions.stem: By Figure 1, moving from the condition in which the experimenter sat beside the participant to the condition in which the instruction came by telephone reduced the proportion reaching level twenty by what percentage of its original value?
questions.explanation: The proportion fell from 80% to 30%, a fall of 50 percentage points. As a share of where it started, that is 50 divided by 80, which is 62.5%.

wrong.A: This is 30 divided by 80, the share of the original proportion that remains, which is what is left rather than what was lost.
wrong.B: This is the fall in percentage points reported as though it were a relative fall, which would only be right if the starting proportion had been 100%.
wrong.D: This divides the fall by the smaller proportion, 50 divided by 30, which gives the rise from the telephone condition up to the seated one.

questions.stem:
On the evidence of this study, which of the following would be expected to lower the proportion of participants reaching level twenty?

I. Raising the number of levels on the dial from twenty to thirty.
II. Replacing the experimenter's live instruction with a recording of it.
III. Seating the experimenter beside the participant rather than across the room.

choices.A: I only
choices.B: II only
choices.C: I and II only
choices.D: I, II and III

questions.explanation: Only item II was manipulated and only item II lowered the proportion, from 80% beside the experimenter to 20% with a recording. Item I was never varied, since every condition used a twenty-level dial, and item III describes the change that produced the highest proportion of all, 80% against 60% across the room.

wrong.A: The number of levels was fixed at twenty throughout, so the study provides no evidence about what a longer dial would do.
wrong.C: Including item I credits the study with a manipulation it never made; lengthening the dial changes what reaching the top level means.
wrong.D: Item III moves the experimenter closer, and Figure 1 shows the proportion rising rather than falling as the experimenter comes nearer.

questions.stem: Which explanation of the low proportion in the recorded-instruction condition is most consistent with the investigators' account?

choices.A: A recording can hold nobody to account, so there is no present authority to whom responsibility for the outcome can be handed.
choices.B: The recorded voice was quieter than a live one, so participants in that condition missed some of the instructions to continue.
choices.C: Participants in that condition had already refused once during practice, and a first refusal makes the next one easier.
choices.D: Acting unobserved produces deindividuation, which releases aggression that the presence of another person restrains.

questions.explanation: The investigators hold that what carries an instruction of this kind is the standing of the person giving it. A recording has no standing, cannot respond to a refusal and cannot take responsibility for what follows, so the participant is left holding it, and six of thirty continued to level twenty.

wrong.B: The recording was made by the same experimenter and played through the same equipment, so there is no reason to think the instruction to continue was any less clear.
wrong.C: No condition included a practice refusal, and participants were assigned at random, so no condition had a history the others lacked.
wrong.D: Deindividuation would predict more severe behaviour when nobody is watching, which is the opposite of the pattern in Figure 1.

questions.stem: Which criticism of the design most weakens the claim that the distance of the instructing person is what produced the differences in Figure 1?

choices.A: Participants were not assigned to conditions at random, so the four groups may have differed in their willingness to obey beforehand.
choices.B: Whether anyone could observe what the participant did changed along with distance, so surveillance and distance are confounded.
choices.C: The outcome is a proportion, and a difference between four proportions cannot be examined statistically.
choices.D: The protests were recorded in advance, so participants in the four conditions were responding to different protests.

questions.explanation: The experimenter beside the participant could see the dial, the experimenter across the room could not, and in the telephone and recorded conditions nobody was present at all. Being watched therefore varies with distance, and either could account for the fall from 80% to 20%.

wrong.A: The passage states that participants were assigned at random, thirty to each condition, which is what makes pre-existing differences an unlikely explanation.
wrong.C: Proportions from four independent groups are compared routinely, and the design gives thirty participants per condition for exactly that purpose.
wrong.D: The protests were identical across conditions, which the passage lists among the features held constant, so they cannot explain any difference between conditions.

questions.stem: What distinguishes the central route to persuasion from the peripheral route?

choices.A: whether the message reaches the reader in writing or in speech
choices.B: whether the attitude the message advocates is favourable or unfavourable
choices.C: whether the person delivering the message is an expert or a fellow student
choices.D: whether the content of the argument is examined and weighed by the reader

questions.explanation: The two routes are distinguished by how much the reader elaborates on the content. On the central route the argument is examined and the attitude follows from its merits; on the peripheral route the attitude follows from cues around the message. The thought counts show the difference directly: about three times as many content-related thoughts where the fee was imminent.

wrong.A: The channel of delivery does not fix the route; a written message can be scrutinised closely or skimmed for cues.
wrong.B: Both routes can produce attitudes in either direction, and the direction of the message is not what defines a route.
wrong.C: The expertise of a source is a peripheral cue, so it is one input to one route rather than the thing that distinguishes the routes.

questions.stem: Students in which cell should hold the attitude that best resists a later counter-argument?

choices.A: fee next term, strong argument, because an attitude built by working through content is anchored in that content
choices.B: fee in ten years, strong argument, because a cue taken on trust leaves nothing for a counter-argument to attack
choices.C: fee next term, weak argument, because effortful processing fixes any attitude firmly whatever its basis
choices.D: fee in ten years, weak argument, because an attitude held without strong feeling is rarely challenged at all

questions.explanation: Attitudes formed by elaborating on the content of an argument are held with more supporting material and so are harder to shift. These students both scrutinised the message, listing 6.4 content-related thoughts on average, and found good material in it, which is the combination that produces a durable attitude.

wrong.B: These students listed only 2.3 content-related thoughts, so their agreement rests on little, and attitudes formed peripherally are the ones that shift most readily.
wrong.C: Elaboration on a weak argument tends to expose its weakness, which is why this cell shows the lowest agreement of all at 4.0.
wrong.D: Resistance to a counter-argument is a property of how an attitude was formed, not of how often it happens to be questioned.

questions.stem: Using the agreement ratings in Table 1, how large is the interaction between argument quality and personal relevance?

choices.A: 0.4 scale points
choices.B: 2.8 scale points
choices.C: 3.2 scale points
choices.D: 3.6 scale points

questions.explanation: Strong against weak is 7.2 minus 4.0, or 3.2 scale points, where the fee begins next term, and 5.6 minus 5.2, or 0.4 scale points, where it begins in ten years. The interaction is the difference between those two differences, 3.2 minus 0.4, which is 2.8 scale points.

wrong.A: This is the effect of argument quality in the low-relevance cells alone, which is one of the two differences the interaction compares.
wrong.C: This is the effect of argument quality in the high-relevance cells alone, and reporting it as the interaction ignores that quality mattered a little even at low relevance.
wrong.D: This adds the two simple effects instead of subtracting one from the other, which inflates the interaction by twice the smaller effect.

questions.stem: The design supports each of the following conclusions EXCEPT:

choices.A: Students who enjoy effortful thinking examine arguments more closely than students who do not.
choices.B: Argument quality mattered more when the fee was to fall on the reader within the year.
choices.C: The number of content-related thoughts tracked personal relevance rather than argument quality.
choices.D: A difference in attitude present before reading is an unlikely explanation of the cell means.

questions.explanation: Enjoyment of effortful thinking is a characteristic of the reader that was neither measured nor manipulated here. What the study varied was the situation, the date the fee would begin, and a situational manipulation cannot establish a claim about differences between kinds of reader.

wrong.B: This is the interaction the data show: 3.2 scale points separate strong from weak where the fee was imminent against 0.4 scale points where it was distant.
wrong.C: The thought counts are about 6 where the fee was imminent and about 2 where it was distant, with little difference between strong and weak within each.
wrong.D: Students were assigned to the four combinations at random, forty to each, which is what makes a pre-existing difference in attitude an unlikely explanation.

questions.stem: Which sociological account is most directly tested by holding the description of the man's conduct constant and varying only the final line?

choices.A: differential association, which holds that conduct is learned within intimate groups
choices.B: the just-world hypothesis, which holds that people are seen to deserve what befalls them
choices.C: social facilitation, which holds that the presence of others alters how a task is performed
choices.D: labelling theory, which holds that the reaction to a label becomes part of what the labelled person faces

questions.explanation: Labelling theory claims that a name attached to conduct brings consequences of its own, over and above the conduct. The design isolates exactly that: three vignettes describe identical conduct and differ only in the label, so any difference in the responses is a reaction to the label.

wrong.A: Differential association concerns how conduct is acquired from those around a person, and nothing in the design varies anybody's associates.
wrong.B: The just-world hypothesis concerns whether misfortune is seen as deserved, which the study did not ask about in any of its four measures.
wrong.C: Social facilitation concerns performance in the presence of others, and respondents performed no task on which they could be facilitated.

questions.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the diagnostic label raising both the recommendation of professional help and the unwillingness to live next door?

choices.A: The label must have made the described conduct sound more severe, since severity drives both responses.
choices.B: Attributing difficulties to a disease of the brain removes blame, and removing blame removes the wish for distance.
choices.C: A label can mark a person as needing treatment and as someone to keep away from, and these are separate judgements.
choices.D: Recommending help and wanting distance are ends of a single scale, so one must fall as the other rises.

questions.explanation: The two measures moved together rather than in opposition: 72% recommended a professional under the diagnostic label and 46% were unwilling to have the man next door, against 41% and 12% with no label. A label can therefore do two things at once, and recommending treatment for a man is not the same as being willing to live beside him.

wrong.A: Every sentence describing what the man did and felt was identical across versions, so the conduct whose severity might be judged was held constant by design.
wrong.B: The table contradicts this: attribution to a brain disease was highest at 68% in the version where unwillingness to live next door was also highest at 46%.
wrong.D: If the two were ends of one scale they could not both rise under the same label, which is precisely what they did.

questions.stem: The investigators note that a man deciding whether to consult anyone must weigh the same reactions the study measured. Which consequence follows most directly?

choices.A: A person who expects to be avoided may conceal symptoms and delay seeking care, even where others would recommend treatment.
choices.B: Because most respondents recommended professional help, a labelled person should meet less delay in reaching treatment.
choices.C: Self-stigma can only operate once treatment has begun, so it has no bearing on whether care is sought.
choices.D: Stigma raises help-seeking, because a named condition is easier to explain to an employer than an unnamed one.

questions.explanation: The reactions measured here are the ones a person anticipates for himself, and anticipated stigma is a cost of being identified as ill. Concealment and delay are the usual way that cost is paid, which is why a high rate of recommending treatment can sit alongside late presentation.

wrong.B: What respondents recommend for someone else is not what the labelled person expects to meet, and the same label raised unwillingness to live next door from 12% to 46%.
wrong.C: Expectations about how others will react are formed before any contact with services, which is when they can deter a person from making contact at all.
wrong.D: Nothing in the table suggests a label makes disclosure easier; it raised social distance from 7.6 to 14.4 on the scale.

questions.stem:
Which of the following limit what this study can establish about how people behave towards those with a mental illness?

I. The outcome is what a respondent says she would do rather than what she does.
II. A respondent may infer the purpose of the study from the single line that differs between versions.
III. The respondents were drawn from an online panel rather than by probability sampling.

choices.A: I only
choices.B: II only
choices.C: I and II only
choices.D: I, II and III

questions.explanation: All three are genuine limits. Stated intentions and conduct diverge, especially where the conduct would be disapproved of; a respondent who guesses the purpose can adjust her answers in either direction; and a panel that is not a probability sample gives no warrant for generalising the percentages to the adult population.

wrong.A: This omits two further limits, one about what respondents may infer from the vignette and one about how the sample was recruited.
wrong.B: Item II is a real limit, but so is the gap between stated intention and conduct, which the investigators themselves raise.
wrong.C: This leaves out the sampling limit, which the passage states plainly in saying the panel is not a probability sample.

questions.stem: By Table 1, a respondent whose parent held a degree was how many times as likely to hold a degree as a respondent whose parents held no qualification?

choices.A: 4.73 times
choices.B: 4.00 times
choices.C: 1.88 times
choices.D: 0.25 times

questions.explanation: The degree column gives 60% for respondents whose parent held a degree and 15% for respondents whose parents held none. Dividing 60 by 15 gives 4.00, which is the multiple the passage quotes when it calls 60 percent four times the 15 percent.

wrong.A: This is 52 divided by 11, the comparison in the column for no qualification, which answers how much more likely the low-origin respondents were to end with nothing.
wrong.C: This is 60 divided by 32, which compares respondents whose parent held a degree with those from a school-certificate household rather than with the lowest origin.
wrong.D: This is 15 divided by 60, the ratio taken the other way round, which expresses the low-origin chance as a fraction of the high-origin one.

questions.stem: The passage notes that a cohort interviewed in middle age is not the cohort that was born. Which pair of demographic processes accounts for the difference between the two?

choices.A: fertility and urbanisation, which set how many children are born and in which places they live
choices.B: mortality and migration, which remove members from a cohort and add members who were born elsewhere
choices.C: fertility and mortality, which together set the size of a birth cohort at the moment it is born
choices.D: urbanisation and globalisation, which redistribute a population within its borders and beyond them

questions.explanation: A birth cohort is closed to further births: once its members have been born, fertility can no longer change who belongs to it. What can change it is death, which removes members, and migration, which adds people born in the same years elsewhere and takes away those who leave. That is why the passage describes composition at interview as the product of births, deaths and migration together, and why 18 percent of these respondents reached the country only after the age of sixteen.

wrong.A: Urbanisation moves people between countryside and town inside a population, so it changes where the cohort's members live rather than which people belong to it.
wrong.C: Fertility fixes how many people are born into the cohort in the first place, which was settled decades before the interview and so cannot be a source of change after birth.
wrong.D: Globalisation names the widening movement of goods, capital and ideas; the movement of people within it is migration, and urbanisation is redistribution inside a country rather than entry or exit.

questions.stem: The share of the cohort holding a degree, 33 percent, exceeds the 25 percent of parental households in which someone held one. What follows?

choices.A: All of the movement in the table is exchange mobility, since each row sums to 100 percent.
choices.B: The table describes intragenerational mobility, since respondents are compared with their own earlier position.
choices.C: Part of the upward movement is structural, since degrees became more common rather than only changing hands between families.
choices.D: No mobility can be inferred from the table, since education rather than income is the measure.

questions.explanation: When the destination distribution differs from the origin distribution, some movement must come from a change in the number of positions available rather than from an exchange of places. A rise from 25 percent to 33 percent means degrees were added to the cohort, so upward movement was possible without anyone moving down.

wrong.A: Exchange mobility alone would require the two distributions to match, and they do not; rows summing to 100 percent is a property of how the table is calculated.
wrong.B: Intragenerational mobility compares positions within one person's life, whereas the table compares a respondent with her parents.
wrong.D: Education is a standard dimension of mobility, and the table reports destinations by origin, which is what a mobility measure is.

questions.stem: Which further finding would best support the claim that the association in Table 1 works through the schools children attend rather than through the home?

choices.A: Respondents whose parents held degrees report more books in the childhood home than other respondents.
choices.B: The share of the cohort holding a degree rose from 25 percent in the parental generation to 33 percent.
choices.C: Respondents who attended fee-paying schools were more likely than others to have a parent with a degree.
choices.D: Among respondents whose schools were funded at the same level per pupil, the association is much weaker.

questions.explanation: A mechanism is supported when holding it constant weakens the association. If the link between parental and own qualification shrinks among respondents whose schools had equal resources, then differences between schools were carrying part of that link.

wrong.A: Books in the home describe a resource inside the family, so this finding supports the home route rather than the schools route.
wrong.B: A change in the overall supply of degrees says nothing about which pathway connects a parent's qualification to a child's.
wrong.C: This shows that school type is associated with parental education, which is a selection into schools and not evidence that schools do the work.

questions.stem:
Which of the following claims about the cohort are supported by the passage?

I. Some respondents received part of their schooling under another country's education system.
II. The cohort is smaller than the one born ten years earlier chiefly because its own members emigrated.
III. The distribution of destinations in Table 1 would be unchanged if the respondents who arrived from abroad were set aside.

choices.A: I only
choices.B: II only
choices.C: I and II only
choices.D: I, II and III

questions.explanation: Item I follows from the 18 percent who arrived after the age of sixteen: a respondent who entered the country at seventeen was taught under another system for the years before that, and her parental qualification was earned there too. Item II is contradicted by the passage, which attributes the fall from 650,000 to 520,000 to the birth rate across the decade and calls emigration slight in both cohorts. Item III cannot be judged at all, because Table 1 is not broken down by place of birth, so nothing shows whether the arrivals' destinations resemble those of the rest.

wrong.B: The passage names the fall in the birth rate as the reason the cohort is smaller and describes emigration as slight, so this item states the explanation the statistical office set aside.
wrong.C: Item I is supported, but item II attributes the smaller cohort to emigration, which the passage rejects in favour of the fall in the birth rate over the intervening decade.
wrong.D: Item III would require the table to be broken down by place of birth, and it is not; the destinations of the respondents who arrived from abroad are nowhere reported separately.

questions.stem: What proportion of the variance in prestige scores across the 90 occupations is accounted for by mean years of schooling?
questions.explanation: The proportion of variance shared by two measures is the square of their correlation. Squaring 0.78 gives 0.608, so mean years of schooling accounts for about 61% of the variance in prestige across the 90 occupations.

wrong.B: This is the variance left over once schooling is accounted for, which is what the two measures do not share.
wrong.C: This squares 0.54, the correlation of prestige with median earnings, so it answers the question for the wrong predictor.
wrong.D: This squares 0.49, the correlation between schooling and earnings, neither of which is the prestige score the question asks about.

questions.stem: The investigators argue for keeping the dimensions of standing apart when social class is measured. Which claim does their argument rest on?

choices.A: Class is settled by ownership of productive property, so measures of prestige add nothing to it.
choices.B: Prestige and earnings must coincide in the long run, because pay reflects what a society values.
choices.C: Once prestige is placed on a single ladder, an occupation cannot rank differently on other dimensions.
choices.D: Prestige, wealth and power are distinguishable dimensions, and an occupation can stand differently on each.

questions.explanation: Treating standing as several dimensions at once, in the manner usually credited to Weber, allows an occupation to be honoured and poorly paid, or well paid and little honoured. The correlation of 0.54 between prestige and earnings leaves ample room for both, which is the investigators' reason for not collapsing the three into one index.

wrong.A: A single criterion of ownership would make the prestige ratings redundant, which is the opposite of what the investigators conclude.
wrong.B: The data contradict this: prestige and earnings correlate at 0.54, and some occupations sit well away from the line relating them.
wrong.C: An occupation's position on a prestige ladder places no constraint on its earnings, which is exactly what the scattered cases show.

questions.stem: What does the coefficient of 0.92 between odd-numbered and even-numbered respondents establish?

choices.A: that the ratings are consistent between halves of the sample, which leaves open whether they capture standing in the community
choices.B: that the ratings are a valid measure of social class, since a measure this consistent must be measuring the right thing
choices.C: that respondents agree because they share one culture, which shows the ladder measures convention rather than standing
choices.D: that 92 percent of the 90 occupations were placed in the same rank order by every respondent in the survey

questions.explanation: Splitting the sample and correlating the two halves is a reliability check: it asks whether the instrument gives the same answer twice. A figure of 0.92 says it does, and says nothing about whether what it gives the same answer about is standing in the community, which is a question of validity.

wrong.B: Reliability does not imply validity. A thermometer reading three degrees too high is perfectly consistent and still wrong.
wrong.C: Shared culture may be why the halves agree, but agreement alone cannot establish that conclusion, and the survey includes no comparison across cultures.
wrong.D: A correlation of 0.92 is not a percentage of occupations ranked identically; it summarises how closely two sets of mean scores move together.

questions.stem: One occupation in the pool has a prestige score of 72 and median earnings in the lowest quarter of the 90. Which description fits it best?

choices.A: absolute deprivation, since its earnings fall below what is needed for necessities
choices.B: downward mobility, since its standing has fallen over the period the survey covers
choices.C: low socioeconomic position overall, since earnings are what finally determine standing
choices.D: status inconsistency, since it stands high on one dimension of standing and low on another

questions.explanation: A prestige score of 72 is well above the middle of the ladder while the earnings are in the bottom quarter, so the two dimensions disagree about where the occupation stands. That disagreement is what status inconsistency names, and it is the reason the investigators resist a single index.

wrong.A: Absolute deprivation is about lacking the means of subsistence, and earnings in the lowest quarter of 90 occupations need not be anywhere near that level.
wrong.B: The survey measured each occupation once, so it contains no information about change over time in any occupation's standing.
wrong.C: Treating earnings as decisive is the assumption the data undercut, since prestige correlates with earnings at only 0.54.

questions.stem: A nineteen-year-old leaves the course her parents chose for her, spends a year working abroad and trying out several political and religious commitments, and now describes a position she says is her own and expects to keep. Which account of her identity fits best?

choices.A: foreclosure, a commitment taken over ready-made from her parents and never held up for examination
choices.B: diffusion, an absence of commitment that is not accompanied by any active search among the alternatives
choices.C: achievement, a commitment settled on by the person herself after a period of searching among alternatives
choices.D: moratorium, an active search among the alternatives that has not yet issued in any settled commitment

questions.explanation: Identity formation is described along two dimensions: whether a person has explored the alternatives and whether she has committed to one of them. This young woman has done both, and in that order, which is the status reached when a period of searching ends in a commitment she regards as hers. The commitment she began with, her parents' choice of course, was the unexamined kind, and leaving it is what started the search.

wrong.A: A foreclosed identity is the one she abandoned: a course chosen by her parents and accepted without a search. She has since examined the alternatives and chosen differently.
wrong.B: Diffusion involves neither searching nor commitment, and she has spent a year searching and arrived at a position she expects to keep.
wrong.D: A moratorium is the searching phase itself, before anything is settled, whereas she describes a position she now holds rather than a question still open.

questions.stem: A tone has been paired with food until the tone alone makes a dog salivate. The tone is then presented repeatedly with no food, and salivation to the tone declines. The decline is an instance of:

choices.A: habituation of an unlearned response to a repeated stimulus
choices.B: spontaneous recovery of a response after a rest interval
choices.C: extinction of a conditioned response that no longer predicts anything
choices.D: latent inhibition of learning about a stimulus already familiar

questions.explanation: Presenting a conditioned stimulus without the unconditioned stimulus that gave it its power reduces the conditioned response, which is extinction. The response can return later without further pairings, which is why extinction is understood as suppression rather than erasure.

wrong.A: Habituation is the waning of an unlearned response to a repeated stimulus, whereas salivation to the tone was acquired by pairing.
wrong.B: Spontaneous recovery is the return of an extinguished response after a rest, so it names what may happen after this decline rather than the decline.
wrong.D: Latent inhibition is slower learning about a stimulus made familiar before any pairing, which is a fact about acquisition rather than about loss.

questions.stem: Lists of long words are ordinarily recalled less well than lists of short words. What should happen to that difference when participants must say an irrelevant syllable aloud throughout presentation and recall of visually shown lists?

choices.A: It should roughly double, because long words carry more meaning and meaning competes with the syllable.
choices.B: It should stay as it is, because the rehearsal system plays no part when words are read rather than heard.
choices.C: It should reverse, because long words become more distinctive when rehearsal is unavailable.
choices.D: It should largely disappear, because the syllable prevents the rehearsal whose speed depends on word length.

questions.explanation: The advantage of short words comes from rehearsal: more short items can be refreshed before they decay. Occupying the articulators with an irrelevant syllable removes rehearsal from the task, so there is no longer a process whose rate depends on how long the words take to say, and the effect of word length goes with it.

wrong.A: Nothing about an irrelevant syllable engages meaning, and the word-length effect is a matter of the time items take to rehearse rather than of what they denote.
wrong.B: Words that are read are ordinarily recoded into a sound-based form and rehearsed there, which is why suppression affects visually presented lists at all.
wrong.C: A reversal would require long words to gain an advantage, and nothing in the task rewards their greater physical distinctiveness.

questions.stem: A man can distinguish blues from yellows but confuses reds with greens at all intensities. The most likely basis of his difficulty is:

choices.A: damage to the opponent cells that carry the blue-yellow comparison
choices.B: a loss of rod function, which removes hue discrimination at low light levels
choices.C: the absence of one cone photopigment, leaving two functioning cone classes
choices.D: an unusually persistent afterimage in the affected part of the spectrum

questions.explanation: Red-green confusion with blue-yellow discrimination intact is the signature of dichromacy from a missing cone photopigment, most often one of the two with overlapping long and middle wavelength sensitivities. With two classes remaining, wavelength differences along one axis can still be signalled and those along the other cannot.

wrong.A: Damage to the blue-yellow comparison would disturb blues and yellows, and it is those that he distinguishes without difficulty.
wrong.B: Rods do not signal hue at all, so losing them affects vision in dim light rather than the discrimination of colours.
wrong.D: An afterimage is a brief consequence of adaptation, not a standing failure to discriminate two regions of the spectrum.

questions.stem: A woman reports surges of intense fear arriving without warning two or three times a month, each lasting about ten minutes, with a pounding heart and a fear that she is dying, and says she now spends much of her time dreading the next one. Which description fits best?

choices.A: generalised anxiety disorder, in which worry is persistent and spread across many areas of life
choices.B: panic disorder, in which unexpected attacks recur and become themselves the object of fear
choices.C: a specific phobia, in which fear is reliably cued by one object or situation
choices.D: obsessive-compulsive disorder, in which intrusive thoughts drive repeated rituals

questions.explanation: Unexpected attacks of short duration with marked bodily symptoms, followed by persistent apprehension about further attacks, is the pattern that defines panic disorder. The fear has taken the attacks themselves as its object, which is what distinguishes it from fear of a situation.

wrong.A: Generalised anxiety involves worry spread across work, health, family and other domains rather than concentrated on the attacks.
wrong.C: A specific phobia requires a cue; these attacks arrive without warning and are not tied to an object or situation.
wrong.D: No intrusive thought or ritual is described, and the dread reported follows the attacks rather than driving any repeated behaviour.

questions.stem: Why does avoiding a feared situation tend to maintain the fear rather than reduce it?

choices.A: The fear is positively reinforced by the sympathy that others offer when avoidance is observed.
choices.B: Escape is negatively reinforced by the relief that follows, so avoidance strengthens while the feared prediction goes untested.
choices.C: The fear response habituates while the situation is avoided, which is why it returns on the next encounter.
choices.D: Avoidance punishes the fear response, and a punished response recovers more strongly later.

questions.explanation: Leaving the situation removes an aversive state, and removing an aversive state reinforces whatever preceded it. So avoidance becomes more likely, and because the person is never present when the predicted catastrophe fails to arrive, the prediction is never disconfirmed.

wrong.A: Attention from others may reinforce complaints, but avoidance is maintained in private as well, which this cannot explain.
wrong.C: Habituation requires exposure to the stimulus; it cannot occur while the situation is being avoided.
wrong.D: Avoidance does not deliver any aversive consequence for being afraid, and a punished response does not recover more strongly for having been punished.

questions.stem: A man who has been treated for depression gives his colleagues a carefully edited account of his two months away from work, and a fuller account to his brother. Which concept best describes what he is doing?

choices.A: role conflict, because the demands of two of his roles cannot both be met
choices.B: deindividuation, because his sense of himself dissolves into the group at work
choices.C: impression management, because each account is shaped for the audience before which it is given
choices.D: a self-fulfilling prophecy, because his colleagues' expectations will bring about what they expect

questions.explanation: Presenting a version of oneself fitted to the audience, and keeping a different version for a backstage audience, is impression management in the dramaturgical sense. The two accounts are both his, and which is given depends on who is watching.

wrong.A: Role conflict arises when two roles make incompatible demands at once, and nothing here requires him to be colleague and brother simultaneously.
wrong.B: Deindividuation is a loss of individual identity within a crowd, whereas he is managing his individual identity with some care.
wrong.D: A self-fulfilling prophecy requires others' expectations to produce the expected conduct, and here it is he who is shaping what they expect.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a feature of stigma as sociologists describe it?

choices.A: a mark that identifies a person as discredited in the eyes of others
choices.B: differential treatment that follows from the mark rather than from conduct
choices.C: a stable trait of the stigmatised person that draws the mark to him
choices.D: the management of information about oneself so as to avoid being marked

questions.explanation: Stigma is treated as a relation between a person and an audience: a mark, the reaction to it, and the work the marked person does to control who knows. Locating it in a trait of the person reverses that account, making the reaction a consequence of the individual rather than of the marking.

wrong.A: A mark that discredits is the starting point of every sociological account of stigma, which is why identical conduct draws different reactions once labelled.
wrong.B: Treatment that follows the label rather than the conduct is the central phenomenon, and vignette studies are designed to isolate it.
wrong.D: Concealment and selective disclosure are standard parts of the account, since a marked person must decide who is told.

questions.stem: A colleague explains to a woman how her health plan's referral system works and which form she must complete to see a specialist. Which kind of social support is this?

choices.A: emotional support, which consists of expressions of care, sympathy and esteem
choices.B: informational support, which consists of advice and guidance about a problem
choices.C: instrumental support, which consists of money, labour or other tangible aid
choices.D: companionship, which consists of shared activity that takes the mind off a problem

questions.explanation: What is transferred is knowledge about how to proceed, which is the defining content of informational support. The colleague neither performs the task, nor offers money, nor addresses how the woman feels about it.

wrong.A: No sympathy or reassurance is offered; the exchange is about the mechanics of a referral.
wrong.C: Instrumental support means doing something tangible, such as completing the form or driving her to the appointment.
wrong.D: Companionship is time spent together for its own sake, which is not what an explanation of a referral system provides.

questions.stem: After a diagnosis becomes known at work, a man finds that colleagues speak to him more slowly and stop asking his opinion, and within a year he describes himself as someone who cannot be relied on. Which concept best captures the change in how he sees himself?

choices.A: self-efficacy, the belief that one can carry out a particular course of action
choices.B: the fundamental attribution error, in which others' conduct is explained by disposition
choices.C: the looking-glass self, in which a person's self-concept takes its shape from how others appear to regard him
choices.D: social loafing, in which individual effort falls when contributions are pooled

questions.explanation: The looking-glass self describes exactly this sequence: the man reads how others treat him, infers their view of him, and comes to hold that view himself. The self-concept here is built from reflected appraisals rather than from any change in what he can do.

wrong.A: Self-efficacy concerns a judgement about a specific task; what has changed is a general view of the kind of person he is.
wrong.B: The attribution error concerns how an observer explains someone else's behaviour, and here the person is revising his view of himself.
wrong.D: Social loafing is a drop in effort within a group task, and nothing describes his effort on a shared task.

questions.stem: Surveys repeatedly find that telling respondents a person's difficulties are caused by a brain disease lowers how much they blame him and raises how dangerous they expect him to be. Which account fits this pattern best?

choices.A: separable components of a stereotype, since a belief about responsibility can change while a belief about danger does not
choices.B: cognitive dissonance, since no respondent can hold a belief about blame and a belief about danger at the same time
choices.C: the just-world hypothesis, since respondents conclude that a man in such a position must have deserved it
choices.D: ingroup bias, since respondents are more generous towards a person they take to resemble themselves

questions.explanation: Beliefs about the cause of a condition, about who is responsible for it and about what the person is likely to do are distinct components of the same stereotype. Shifting one does not drag the others with it, which is why a campaign that lowers blame can leave expected dangerousness untouched or raise it.

wrong.B: Dissonance requires beliefs that contradict one another, and a man can coherently be held blameless and thought unpredictable.
wrong.C: On a just-world account lowered blame should follow from the person being seen as deserving, which is the reverse of what the pattern shows.
wrong.D: Ingroup bias would predict differences between respondents of different groups rather than a change produced by varying the stated cause.

questions.stem: In a survey of 750 adults, 300 said they would be unwilling to work closely with someone who had been treated for a psychotic illness. What are the odds that a respondent drawn at random from this survey holds that view?
questions.explanation: Odds are the number holding the view divided by the number not holding it, which is 300 divided by 450, or 0.67. The probability, by contrast, is 300 divided by 750, and the two coincide only as the probability approaches zero.

wrong.A: This is the probability, 300 out of 750, which divides by the whole sample rather than by those who do not hold the view.
wrong.C: This inverts the odds, dividing 450 by 300, and so gives the odds against holding the view.
wrong.D: This is 750 divided by 300, the reciprocal of the probability, which is neither a probability nor a set of odds.

questions.stem: A country's population pyramid has a narrow base, a bulge through the middle years and a broad top, and its births have run below replacement level for thirty years. Which description of its position in the demographic transition fits?

choices.A: a late position, with births and deaths both low, an ageing age structure and a population that may begin to shrink
choices.B: an early position, with births and deaths both high, so the pyramid has a wide base and very few old people in it
choices.C: a position in which deaths have fallen while births remain high, which is when a population grows at its fastest
choices.D: a position in which births have begun to fall from a high level, so growth continues but at a slackening rate

questions.explanation: The demographic transition runs from high birth and death rates, through a phase in which deaths fall first and the population grows quickly, to low rates of both. A narrow base means few children are being born; a broad top means most members of earlier cohorts have survived into old age; and thirty years below replacement means the cohorts entering the pyramid are smaller than those leaving it. That is the late pattern, and the one in which a population can decline with no rise at all in mortality.

wrong.B: An early position shows the opposite pyramid, a wide base of children under a narrow top, because high death rates stop most of each cohort from reaching old age.
wrong.C: This is the phase of fastest growth, when falling deaths meet births that are still high, and it widens the base of the pyramid rather than narrowing it.
wrong.D: Births falling from a high level still leaves each arriving cohort large; three decades below replacement level is well past the point where growth merely slows.

questions.stem: A city's population grew by 40,000 people between two censuses. An investigator wants to know how much of that growth was natural increase and how much was people moving in. Which approach best separates the two?

choices.A: compare the city's totals at the two censuses and assign the growth to whichever component is larger nationally
choices.B: subtract the deaths registered in the city from the births registered there, and compare that figure with the growth
choices.C: compare the share of residents under fifteen at the two censuses, since a growing population must be a younger one
choices.D: ask a sample of current residents how long each has lived in the city and project those answers back to the first census

questions.explanation: Growth over an interval is natural increase, births minus deaths, plus net migration, arrivals minus departures. Registers of births and deaths measure the first term directly, so the second can be recovered as whatever is left of the 40,000 once natural increase has been taken out. Estimating net migration as that residual is the standard approach, because arrivals and departures are nowhere counted as completely as births and deaths are.

wrong.A: The national balance between the two components says nothing about one city, which may be gaining migrants while the country as a whole grows through natural increase.
wrong.C: A population can grow younger through the arrival of young adults and the children they then have, so the age structure cannot tell natural increase and migration apart.
wrong.D: A sample of current residents omits everyone who left or died during the interval, and length of residence records no births and no deaths at all.

questions.stem: A region funds each school district from taxes on property within it, so districts with cheaper housing spend less per pupil, although no official intends that result. The disadvantage to pupils in those districts is best described as:

choices.A: institutional discrimination, since it follows from the ordinary operation of a rule rather than from anyone's intent
choices.B: individual prejudice, since the disadvantage must be traced to the attitudes of the officials who apply the rule
choices.C: relative poverty, since it is defined by how the families in those districts compare with families elsewhere
choices.D: a meritocratic allocation, since each district receives in proportion to what its residents have contributed

questions.explanation: Discrimination built into a rule produces unequal outcomes whatever the attitudes of those administering it, and a funding formula tied to local property values is a standard example. The disadvantage is reproduced by the institution's routine operation, which is why removing prejudiced individuals would not remove it.

wrong.B: The description states that no official intends the result, and institutional discrimination is precisely the form that needs no prejudiced individual.
wrong.C: Relative poverty is a way of measuring household income against a social standard, not a description of how a public service is allocated.
wrong.D: Calling the outcome merited assumes that what residents can contribute is the right basis for a child's schooling, which is the point at issue rather than a description of it.
